claim: The INTACT method using twi-INTACT and elav-INTACT fly lines did not affect Drosophila embryonic development.
source: Co-expression of both transgenes in Drosophila embryos, which did not affect development (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1H), resulted in cell type-specific biotinylation of nuclei in vivo (Figure 1A–C').
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1H showing normal development patterns.

claim: Mef2-positive nuclei and mesodermal marker genes like Mef2 and nautilus were detected almost exclusively in the mesodermal collection using INTACT.
source: Mesodermal or neuronal nuclei were efficiently isolated using Streptavidin-coated beads, as we detected Mef2-positive nuclei and concomitantly mesodermal marker gene expression like Mef2 and nautilus (nau) almost exclusively in the mesodermal collection (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating marker gene expression patterns.

claim: Elav-labelled neuronal nuclei and neuronal marker genes like eagle and elav were found highly enriched in the neuronal fraction only.
source: while Elav-labelled neuronal nuclei and neuronal marker genes like eagle (eg) and elav were found highly enriched in the neuronal fraction only (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: In total, transcripts corresponding to 5652 coding genes were identified for the early mesodermal nuclei populations.
source: In total, transcripts (containing >5 RPKM) corresponding to 5652 coding genes were identified for the early mesodermal, 5716 coding genes for late mesodermal, 6752 coding genes for the early neuronal and 6182 coding genes for the late neuronal nuclei populations
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis with specific RPKM threshold criteria.

claim: The transcriptome of the mesodermal lineage was clearly distinct from the neuronal one at both time points with Pearson correlation coefficients of r = 0.72 for stages10-13 and r = 0.53 for stages14-17.
source: Pearson correlation coefficient analysis revealed that the transcriptome of the mesodermal lineage was clearly distinct from the neuronal one at both time points (r = 0.72 for stages10-13; r = 0.53 for stages14-17) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis with specific correlation coefficients provided.

claim: GO term classification revealed a significant enrichment of processes typical for the respective lineage (mesoderm both stages: p-value<2.2e-16, neuronal stages10-13: p-value<1.26e-6, neuronal stages14-17: p-value<5.3e-5).
source: Importantly, GO term classification revealed a significant enrichment of processes typical for the respective lineage (mesoderm both stages: p-value<2.2e-16, neuronal stages10-13: p-value<1.26e-6, neuronal stages14-17: p-value<5.3e-5) (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of GO term enrichment with specific p-values provided.

claim: Global gene expression in the mesodermal lineage changed substantially over the selected time points with a Pearson correlation coefficient of r = 0.78.
source: In addition to elucidating differences in tissue profiles, Pearson correlation coefficient analysis also showed that global gene expression in the mesodermal lineage changed substantially over the selected time points (r = 0.78 for mesoderm stages10-13 + stages14-17) (Figure 1F and H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by Pearson correlation analysis comparing different developmental stages.

claim: In contrast to the mesoderm, the neuronal transcriptomes were very similar at both developmental time frames.
source: PCA analysis also showed that in contrast to the mesoderm the neuronal transcriptomes were very similar at both developmental time frames (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: The claim is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: The similarity of neuronal transcriptomes at both time points is assumed to be a consequence of the earlier onset of nervous system differentiation.
source: which we assumed to be a consequence of the earlier onset of nervous system differentiation (Bate, 2009; Hartenstein, 1993).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ubx ChIP-seq sequencing was performed in biological duplicates with Pearson correlation coefficients of r = 0.94–0.96.
source: The sequencing was performed in biological duplicates and Pearson correlation coefficient analysis revealed a high similarity of the samples (r = 0.94–0.96).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of replicate ChIP-seq experiments.

claim: Ubx binds to the decapentaplegic (dpp) enhancer in mesodermal but not neuronal nuclei.
source: We found Ubx to interact with both enhancers using chromatin from INTACT sorted mesodermal but not neuronal nuclei (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing differential binding patterns in different lineages.

claim: Ubx binds to the β-Tubulin at 60D (βTub60D) enhancer in mesodermal but not neuronal nuclei.
source: We found Ubx to interact with both enhancers using chromatin from INTACT sorted mesodermal but not neuronal nuclei (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), showing that our data reflected Ubx interactions in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ubx interacted with different genomic regions in the mesodermal and neuronal tissue lineages.
source: However, this analysis also uncovered that Ubx, which is known to have different functions in the developing mesoderm and nervous system (Enriquez et al., 2010; Hessinger et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 1995; Miller et al., 2001) and which interacted with different genomic regions in the two tissue lineages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A), targeted many genes in both tissue lineages (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis and citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Only 27% to 36% of the Ubx chromatin interactions occurred in the vicinity of genes actively transcribed either in the mesodermal or neuronal lineages at the different stages.
source: We found that only 27% to 36% of the Ubx chromatin interactions occurred in the vicinity of genes actively transcribed either in the mesodermal or neuronal lineages at the different stages (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: More than 60% of Ubx interactions with active genes occurred at intron, intergenic and distal enhancer regions.
source: with more than 60% of these interactions occurring at intron, intergenic and distal enhancer regions (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic location analysis of ChIP-seq peaks shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A large portion of the Ubx chromatin interactions (64% to 73%) were close to inactive genes in the two lineages.
source: In contrast, a large portion of the Ubx chromatin interactions (64% to 73%) were close to inactive genes in the two lineages (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: There was a substantial overrepresentation of GO terms characteristic for the respective lineage among the Ubx targeted and expressed genes (mesoderm: p-value 2.2e-16, neuronal stages10-13: p-value 2.2e-16, neuronal stages14-17: p-value 1.004e-9).
source: By determining the gene functions associated with Ubx interactions, we found a substantial overrepresentation of GO terms characteristic for the respective lineage among the Ubx targeted and expressed genes (mesoderm: p-value 2.2e-16, neuronal stages10-13: p-value 2.2e-16, neuronal stages14-17: p-value 1.004e-9) (Figure 2C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis with specific p-values.

claim: Ubx interactions at inactive genes occurred frequently at genes controlling processes active in other lineages.
source: while Ubx interactions at inactive genes occurred frequently at genes controlling processes active in other lineages (Figure 2—figure supplements 1B–2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term analysis of inactive genes bound by Ubx.

claim: Ectodermal and neuronal but not mesodermal GO terms were highly enriched among the inactive genes bound by Ubx in the early mesodermal lineage (neuronal GO-terms: p-value 0.0008442, ectoderm GO terms: p-value 0.01196, mesodermal: p-value 0.7118).
source: For example, ectodermal and neuronal but not mesodermal GO terms (p-value 0.7118) were highly enriched among the inactive genes bound by Ubx in the early mesodermal lineage (neuronal GO-terms: p-value 0.0008442, ectoderm GO terms: p-value 0.01196).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis with specific p-values for different lineage-related terms.

claim: Ubx and Mef2 binding profiles were rather similar in their correlation with gene classes represented among active and inactive genes.
source: WEADE analysis of genes bound by these two TFs revealed that Tin interactions did not reflect very well the gene classes represented among the active and inactive genes, while Ubx and Mef2 profiles were rather similar (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by WEADE analysis comparing binding profiles of different transcription factors.

claim: Tin preferentially interacted with genes controlling stem cell processes irrespective of whether these genes were actively transcribed or silent.
source: Indeed, Tin preferentially interacted with genes controlling stem cell processes irrespective of whether these genes were actively transcribed or silent (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by WEADE analysis of Tin binding patterns.

claim: The broadly expressed Hox TF Ubx played a prominent role in orchestrating the transcriptional program in the mesodermal and neuronal lineages.
source: In sum, these results illustrated that the broadly expressed Hox TF Ubx played a prominent role in orchestrating the transcriptional program in the mesodermal (and neuronal) lineages.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comprehensive binding and expression analysis presented.

claim: A substantial fraction of Ubx interactions were found in the vicinity of inactive genes, which encoded many mesoderm-unrelated functions.
source: In addition, our analysis revealed that a substantial fraction of Ubx interactions were found in the vicinity of inactive genes, which encoded many mesoderm-unrelated functions.
evidence: The claim is supported by the overlap analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data combined with GO term analysis.

claim: One important function of Ubx in tissue development could be the repression of alternative transcriptional programs, which instruct the development of other lineages.
source: Thus, we hypothesized that one important function of Ubx in tissue development could be the repression of alternative transcriptional programs, which instruct the development of other lineages.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that Ubx binds to inactive genes encoding alternative lineage functions.

claim: The GFP-Ubx fusion protein is functional and can rescue Ubx mutants.
source: Intactness of the fusion protein in the homozygous viable GFP-Ubx fly line was verified by rescuing Ubx mutants using the GFP-Ubx allele (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic rescue experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H–L.

claim: Co-localization of GFP and Ubx protein expression in GFP-Ubx embryos confirmed a precise expression control of the fusion protein.
source: Co-localization of GFP and Ubx protein expression in GFP-Ubx embryos (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D) confirmed a precise expression control of the fusion protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-localization.

claim: Ubiquitous degradation of GFP-Ubx using the arm-GAL4 driver resulted in a strong reduction of GFP-Ubx protein levels.
source: We first functionally verified the system by ubiquitously degrading the GFP-Ubx fusion protein using the armadillo (arm)-GAL4 driver, which resulted in a strong reduction of GFP-Ubx protein levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–G,O)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data.

claim: Ubiquitous degradation of GFP-Ubx resulted in animals resembling the Ubx null mutant phenotype.
source: and in animals resembling the Ubx null mutant phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1M,N) (Lewis, 1978).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis and citation to the original Ubx mutant description.

claim: Mesoderm-specific degradation of GFP-Ubx using the Mef2-GAL4 driver substantially decreased GFP-Ubx protein accumulation in the mesoderm.
source: In a next step, we applied deGradFP to specifically interfere with Ubx function in the mesoderm using the Mef2-GAL4 driver (Zars et al., 2000). This combination substantially decreased GFP-Ubx protein accumulation in the mesoderm (Figure 3C,D,G)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data showing reduced protein levels.

claim: Mesoderm-specific degradation of Ubx decreased the expression of the direct Ubx target gene dpp in the visceral mesoderm.
source: and the expression of the direct Ubx target gene dpp in the visceral mesoderm (Figure 3H–J) (Manak et al., 1994; Zaffran et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data and citations to previous studies identifying dpp as a Ubx target.

claim: Mesoderm-specific degradation of Ubx resulted in the loss of the third midgut constriction.
source: Consequently, we only observed the well-described loss of the third midgut constriction in these embryos (Figure 3E,F), which is caused by the absence of Ubx activity in this tissue (Bienz et al., 1988)
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis and citation to previous studies.

claim: All non-mesodermal tissues were unaffected by mesoderm-specific degradation of Ubx.
source: while all non-mesodermal tissues were unaffected (Figure 3E–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis showing tissue-specific effects.

claim: The Mef2-GAL4 driver activity starts at embryonic stage 7.
source: Due to the activity of the Mef2-GAL4 driver starting at embryonic stage 7 (Zars et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the original characterization of the Mef2-GAL4 driver.

claim: Significant reduction of Ubx protein levels in the mesoderm occurred only at stage 12 when using the Mef2-GAL4 driver.
source: which resulted in significant reduction of Ubx protein levels in the mesoderm only at stage 12 (Figure 3C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal analysis of protein degradation shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Comparison of the Ubx depleted and control mesodermal transcriptomes revealed a differential expression of 2845 genes.
source: Comparison of the Ubx depleted and control mesodermal transcriptomes revealed a differential expression of 2845 genes, with 1393 genes showing increased mRNA accumulation, including Fasciclin 2 (Fas2), ventral veins lacking (vvl), Neurotrophin 1 (NT1) and myospheroid (mys), while 1452 genes exhibited reduced expression, including βTub60D, Ankyrin 2 (Ank2) and Notchless (Nle) (Figure 3K).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: 55% (791/1452) of the genes with reduced expression and 70% (978/1393) of the genes with increased expression were bound by Ubx in mesodermal nuclei in wild-type embryos.
source: In total, 55% (791/1452) of the genes with reduced and 70% (978/1393) of the genes with increased expression were bound by Ubx in mesodermal nuclei in wild-type embryos, implying that the majority of expression changes were a direct consequence of altered Ubx chromatin interactions.
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: The majority of expression changes in Ubx depleted mesoderm were a direct consequence of altered Ubx chromatin interactions.
source: implying that the majority of expression changes were a direct consequence of altered Ubx chromatin interactions.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high percentage of differentially expressed genes that are also bound by Ubx.

claim: Down-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesoderm mostly functioned in general cell processes like translation, RNA processing and gene expression.
source: A detailed analysis of biological GO terms showed that down-regulated genes mostly functioned in general cell processes like translation, RNA processing and gene expression (Figure 3L)
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis of down-regulated genes.

claim: Up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesoderm controlled primarily lineage-specific functions like central nervous system, axon and cutical development.
source: while up-regulated genes controlled primarily lineage-specific functions like central nervous system, axon and cutical development (Figure 3L).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis of up-regulated genes.

claim: Translation and cell cycle processes were directly activated by Ubx in the mesoderm.
source: For example, translation and cell cycle processes, which were enriched among the expressed as well as Ubx bound active genes in the control transcriptome, were now represented among the transcripts with reduced accumulation in the absence of Ubx (Figure 3M), supporting that these processes were directly activated by Ubx.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from WEADE analysis showing correlation between Ubx binding and gene expression changes.

claim: Stimulus and signalling related processes were overrepresented among the genes with enhanced activity in the absence of Ubx.
source: On the other hand, stimulus and signalling related processes, which were only to a minor extent represented among the genes expressed in the mesoderm, were found enriched among the genes with enhanced activity in the absence of Ubx (Figure 3M).
evidence: The claim is supported by WEADE analysis of up-regulated genes.

claim: Stimulus and signalling processes were overrepresented among the inactive genes bound by Ubx in control mesodermal nuclei, consistent with a repressive function of Ubx.
source: Consistent with a repressive function of Ubx, these processes were overrepresented among the inactive genes bound by Ubx in control mesodermal nuclei (Figure 3M).
evidence: The claim is supported by WEADE analysis showing correlation between Ubx binding at inactive genes and their de-repression upon Ubx loss.

claim: Differentiation processes were enriched among the genes up-regulated in the absence of Ubx.
source: Intriguingly, we found differentiation processes to be enriched among the genes up-regulated in the absence of Ubx (Figure 3L,M).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Processes controlling the development of lineages other than the mesoderm, including the neuronal, ectodermal and endodermal lineages, were predominantly represented among the up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesodermal cells.
source: Analysing differentiation processes revealed that processes controlling the development of lineages other than the mesoderm, including the neuronal, ectodermal end endodermal lineages, were predominantly represented among the up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesodermal cells (Figure 3L, Figure 3—figure supplement 1P)
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis of up-regulated genes.

claim: The enrichment of alternative lineage processes among up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesoderm was significantly higher than expected by chance (neuronal and ectoderm: p-value<2.2e-16, endoderm and gut structures: p-value 5.04e-14).
source: which was significantly higher than expected by chance (neuronal and ectoderm: p-value<2.2e-16, endoderm and gut structures: p-value 5.04e-14).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of GO term enrichment.

claim: 56% (774/1393) of the up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesoderm were normally expressed and functional in the neuronal lineage in the wild type situation.
source: Comparing these genes to the neuronal transcriptomes, which we have generated, showed that 56% (774/1393) of the up-regulated genes were normally expressed and functional in the neuronal lineage in the wild type situation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1P)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of up-regulated genes with neuronal transcriptome data.

claim: The remaining 44% (617/1393) of up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesoderm were active in other lineages according to GO term prediction.
source: while the remaining 44% (617/1393) were active in other lineages according to GO term prediction (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on GO term analysis of genes not expressed in the neuronal lineage.

claim: Ubx controlled a large number of genes encoding diverse functions.
source: Taken together, these results showed that Ubx controlled a large number of genes encoding diverse functions.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on the comprehensive RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: The strong correlation between Ubx binding with specifically repressed or activated classes of genes suggested that Ubx exerts a dominant influence over the mesodermal transcriptome.
source: The strong correlation between Ubx binding with specifically repressed or activated classes of genes suggested that Ubx indeed exerts a dominant influence over the mesodermal transcriptome at the two stages analysed.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation analysis between Ubx binding and gene expression patterns.

claim: Ubx repressed many genes controlling the establishment of non-mesodermal, alternative lineages.
source: In addition, this analysis highlighted that Ubx repressed many genes controlling the establishment of non-mesodermal, alternative lineages
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term analysis of up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesoderm.

claim: Ubx could have a pivotal role in restricting the developmental potential of cells and tissues, thereby ensuring that lineages adopt a unique identity.
source: indicating that Ubx could have a pivotal role in restricting the developmental potential of cells and tissues, thereby ensuring that lineages adopt a unique identity.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation that Ubx represses alternative lineage genes.

claim: In the early mesoderm about 30% of all Ubx chromatin interactions overlapped with H3K27me3 peaks and about 20% with H3K27ac peaks.
source: This analysis revealed that in the early mesoderm about 30% of all Ubx chromatin interactions overlapped with H3K27me3 peaks and about 20% with H3K27ac peaks
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq data for Ubx and histone modifications.

claim: In the late mesoderm 40% of all Ubx chromatin interactions overlapped with H3K27me3 peaks and 73% with H3K27ac peaks.
source: while in the late mesoderm 40% of all Ubx chromatin interactions overlapped with H3K27me3 peaks and 73% with H3K27ac peaks (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: About 70% of Ubx interactions with repressive chromatin occurred at inactive genes irrespective of the developmental stage.
source: Ubx interactions with repressive chromatin were predictive of gene activity, as about 70% of these occurred at inactive genes irrespective of the developmental stage (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of Ubx/H3K27me3 binding with gene expression data.

claim: Ubx interactions with repressive chromatin at inactive genes were associated with functions unrelated to the mesoderm (neuronal: p-value 7.05e-5–6.59e-6, ectoderm: p-value 4.80e-5–5.21e-7).
source: which we found again associated with functions unrelated to the mesoderm (neuronal: p-value 7.05e-5–6.59e-6, ectoderm: p-value 4.80e-5–5.21e-7) (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis with specific p-values.

claim: Less than half of the Ubx interactions with active chromatin occurred close to active genes.
source: In contrast, less than half of the Ubx interactions with active chromatin occurred close to active genes (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ubx interactions with active chromatin at active genes were enriched for mesoderm-related functions.
source: which were as before enriched for mesoderm-related functions (Figure 4C)
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Only a minor fraction (about 20%) of the Ubx bound repressive chromatin regions occurred at promoters, while the majority was found at putative distal enhancers, in introns and intergenic regions.
source: Organizing chromatin environment by genomic location revealed that only a minor fraction (about 20%) of the Ubx bound repressive chromatin regions occurred at promoters, while the majority was found at putative distal enhancers, in introns and intergenic regions in both developmental time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic location analysis of ChIP-seq peaks.

claim: In total, 1216 H3K27me3 peaks and 1480 H3K27ac peaks located in gene regulatory regions changed their chromatin state in the absence of Ubx.
source: In total, 1216 H3K27me3 peaks and 1480 H3K27ac peaks located in gene regulatory regions, which corresponded to 2768 genes, changed their chromatin state in the absence of Ubx, as they experienced either a reduction/loss or an increase/gain in tri-methylation/acetylation at lysine 27 of histone 3 (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis of histone ChIP-seq data.

claim: 80% of genomic regions that changed histone marks in the absence of Ubx possessed an Ubx binding peak in control mesodermal cells.
source: Importantly, 80% of these genomic regions possessed an Ubx binding peak in control mesodermal cells, indicating that Ubx was critically required for establishing or maintaining the majority of these histone marks.
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of regions with histone changes and Ubx binding sites.

claim: Ubx was critically required for establishing or maintaining the majority of histone marks that changed in its absence.
source: indicating that Ubx was critically required for establishing or maintaining the majority of these histone marks.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high percentage of regions with histone changes that are also bound by Ubx.

claim: 1058 genes were primed for gene expression as they experienced a loss/reduction of H3K27me3 and/or gain/increase of H3K27ac in their regulatory regions in the absence of Ubx.
source: Intriguingly, 1058 of these genes were primed for gene expression, as they experienced a loss/reduction of H3K27me3 and/or gain/increase of H3K27ac in their regulatory regions (Figure 4D)
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of histone mark changes at gene regulatory regions.

claim: 164 genes that were primed for activation by histone changes were indeed up-regulated in the mesodermal lineage in the absence of Ubx.
source: and 164 of them were indeed up-regulated in the mesodermal lineage in the absence of Ubx (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of genes with histone changes and RNA-seq data.

claim: The 164 genes with histone changes towards activation that were up-regulated were highly enriched for processes critically controlling the development of lineages other than the mesoderm (neuronal: p-value<2.2e-16, ectoderm: p-value 1.36e-12, endoderm and gut structures: p-value<2.2e-16).
source: Consistent with previous results, these 164 genes were highly enriched for processes critically controlling the development of lineages other than the mesoderm (neuronal: p-value<2.2e-16, ectoderm: p-value 1.36e-12, endoderm and gut structures: p-value<2.2e-16) (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis with specific p-values.

claim: The majority of genes primed for activation (894 of 1058) remained silent on the RNA level when Ubx was lineage-specifically degraded.
source: One result that puzzled us was that the majority of genes primed for activation (894 of 1058) remained silent on the RNA level when Ubx was lineage-specifically degraded (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of genes with histone changes and RNA-seq data.

claim: H3K27ac marks were equally increased at promoters and enhancers of genes unchanged or up-regulated in the absence of Ubx.
source: We found that H3K27ac marks were equally increased at promoters and enhancers of genes unchanged or up-regulated in the absence of Ubx (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of histone mark changes at different genomic regions.

claim: H3K27me3 marks were significantly decreased at enhancers as well as promoters of up-regulated genes in the absence of Ubx.
source: However, while H3K27me3 marks were significantly decreased at enhancers as well as promoters of up-regulated genes
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of histone mark changes.

claim: Unchanged genes showed a significant increase in H3K27me3 at their enhancers in the absence of Ubx.
source: unchanged genes showed a significant increase in H3K27me3 at their enhancers (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of histone mark changes shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Ubx played a major role in repressing the expression of alternative fate genes by controlling the deposition/maintenance of H3K27me3 marks at enhancers.
source: As a high proportion of Ubx and H3K27me3 peaks co-occurred at enhancers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), this result revealed that Ubx played a major role in repressing the expression of alternative fate genes by controlling the deposition/maintenance of H3K27me3 marks at enhancers.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the correlation between Ubx binding, H3K27me3 marks at enhancers, and gene repression.

claim: Ubx mediated the repression of genes encoding non-mesodermal functions by controlling the epigenetic status, in particular H3K27me3, at Ubx bound chromatin sites located in enhancers.
source: In sum, these results showed that Ubx mediated the repression of genes encoding non-mesodermal functions by controlling the epigenetic status, in particular H3K27me3, at Ubx bound chromatin sites located in enhancers.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement based on the histone modification analysis.

claim: Motifs for Ubx, Extradenticle (Exd), and Trithorax-like (Trl) were among the highest ranking motifs in both Ubx/H3K27me3 and Ubx/H3K27ac regions.
source: We found in both cases motifs for Ubx, Extradenticle (Exd), a TALE class homeobox TF functioning as Hox cofactor in invertebrates and vertebrates (Mann et al., 2009; Moens and Selleri, 2006), and Trithorax-like (Trl), a GAGA factor activating and repressing gene expression by chromatin modification (Kingston and Tamkun, 2014), among the highest ranking motifs.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis and citations to previous literature on these factors.

claim: The DNA binding motif for Pleiohomeotic (Pho) was specifically enriched only among the co-occurring Ubx and H3K27me3 binding events.
source: In contrast, the DNA binding motif for the zinc finger protein Pleiohomeotic (Pho) was specifically enriched only among the co-occurring Ubx and H3K27me3 binding events (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the absence of Pho, H3K27me3 marks were reduced in Polycomb regions and redistributed to heterochromatin.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown just recently that in the absence of Pho, which recruits PcGs to PREs (Frey et al., 2016; Fritsch et al., 1999; Kahn et al., 2014), H3K27me3 marks were reduced in Polycomb regions and redistributed to heterochromatin (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study on Pho function.

claim: Pho was found expressed in mesodermal cells also expressing Ubx.
source: Consistent with this idea Pho was found expressed in mesodermal cells also expressing Ubx (Figure 5B-C'').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing co-expression.

claim: A weak interaction of Ubx and Pho proteins was confirmed in a complex in vitro and in vivo by co-immunoprecipitation experiments.
source: Furthermore, we confirmed a weak interaction of Ubx and Pho proteins in a complex in vitro and in vivo by performing co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) experiments in cellulo using Drosophila S2R + cells transfected with tagged versions of Ubx and Pho as well as in vivo using GFP-Ubx embryos (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP experiments in cell culture and embryos.

claim: 4814 chromatin regions (which represent 62% of the Ubx and 12% of the Pho binding events) were co-bound by Ubx and Pho and marked by H3K27me3 in stage 14–17 mesodermal cells.
source: We found 4814 chromatin regions (which represent 62% of the Ubx and 12% of the Pho binding events) to be co-bound by Ubx and Pho and marked by H3K27me3 in stage 14–17 mesodermal cells (Figures 5D and 6A)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq data for Ubx, Pho, and H3K27me3.

claim: 40% of Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 binding events occurred at promoters and 49% at enhancers.
source: with 40% of these events occurring at promoters and 49% at enhancers (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic location analysis of co-bound regions.

claim: 66% (3099/4715) of the genes bound by Ubx and Pho as well as marked by H3K27me3 were not expressed in the mesoderm.
source: Consistent with the reported role of Pho in transcriptional repression (Frey et al., 2016; Fritsch et al., 1999; Kahn et al., 2014), 66% (3099/4715) of the genes bound by Ubx and Pho as well as marked by H3K27me3 were not expressed in the mesoderm (Figure 5D)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data, and citations to previous studies on Pho function.

claim: The majority of inactive genes bound by Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 encoded non-mesodermal and stem cell-related functions (neuronal: p-value 1,62e-4, ectodermal: 1,71e-5).

evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis with specific p-values.

claim: The 1616 genes bound by Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 but expressed in mesodermal cells encoded gene functions controlling processes typical for the tissue type and developmental stage.
source: This was different for the remaining 1616 genes also bound by Ubx and Pho and marked by H3K27me3 but expressed in mesodermal cells, as they encoded gene functions controlling processes typical for the tissue type and developmental stage (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis.

claim: Chromatin regions associated with inactive genes had a higher coverage of H3K27me3 and lower coverage of H3K27ac at shared Ubx/Pho binding regions compared to active genes.
source: By analysing the distribution of H3K27me3 and H3K27ac at regulatory regions, we discovered that those chromatin regions associated with inactive genes had a higher coverage of H3K27me3 and lower coverage of H3K27ac at shared Ubx/Pho binding regions, while it was the opposite for active genes (Figure 5I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of histone mark distribution.

claim: The canonical Pho binding motif was found overrepresented only among the Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 chromatin regions associated with genes inactive in the mesoderm.
source: Furthermore, the canonical Pho binding motif was found overrepresented only among the Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 chromatin regions associated with genes inactive in the mesoderm (Figure 5H)
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: DNA binding motifs for Ubx, Exd and Trl were overrepresented in Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 chromatin regions associated with inactive as well as active genes.
source: while other DNA binding motifs, including the ones for Ubx, Exd and Trl, were overrepresented in Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 chromatin regions associated with inactive as well as active genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Ubx and Pho interacted with the same chromatin regions to control gene expression.
source: This result suggested that Ubx and Pho could interact with the same chromatin regions to control gene expression
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the co-occurrence of Ubx and Pho binding and their protein interaction.

claim: All five Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci tested experienced a dramatic loss of Pho binding when Ubx was degraded.
source: Strikingly, all five Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci, which were co-bound by Ubx and Pho in the presence of Ubx (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B), experienced a dramatic loss of Pho binding when Ubx was degraded (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR experiments comparing Pho binding in control and Ubx depleted conditions.

claim: Pho binding to Pho-only control loci remained unaffected when Ubx was degraded.
source: In contrast, Pho binding to Pho-only control loci remained unaffected (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR experiments on control loci.

claim: Pho expression levels were unaltered in the absence of Ubx.
source: As Pho expression levels were unaltered in the absence of Ubx (Figure 7C)
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Ubx is required to stabilize Pho binding to chromatin of H3K27me3 marked loci.
source: we concluded that Ubx is required to stabilize Pho binding to chromatin of H3K27me3 marked loci.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the loss of Pho binding when Ubx is depleted despite unchanged Pho expression.

claim: The expression of vnd and Ptx1 was significantly increased in the mesoderm of Mef2 >Nslmb,GFP-Ubx embryos compared to control embryos.
source: In line with this hypothesis, we found the expression of vnd and Ptx1, which were normally not or only weakly expressed in mesodermal cells of stage 16 control embryos (Figure 6C,D,I,J) to be significantly increased in the mesoderm of Mef2 >Nslmb,GFP-Ubx embryos (Figure 6E,F,I,J, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and quantification data.

claim: In the absence of Pho, H3K27me3 enrichment was decreased.
source: It has been recently reported that in the absence of Pho H3K27me3 enrichment was decreased (Brown et al., 2018; Kraushaar et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies on Pho function.

claim: H3K27me3 levels at the HGTX and ham associated Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci were significantly decreased in Ubx depleted mesodermal nuclei.
source: and consistently, we found that H3K27me3 levels at the HGTX and ham associated Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci were significantly decreased in Ubx depleted mesodermal nuclei (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H3K27ac levels remained unaffected at the HGTX associated Ubx binding locus in Ubx depleted mesodermal nuclei.
source: Importantly, while H3K27ac levels remained unaffected at the HGTX associated Ubx binding locus
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: H3K27ac levels were increased at the ham associated Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 region in Ubx depleted mesodermal nuclei.
source: they were increased at the ham associated Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 region (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: H3K27me3 levels at Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci associated with the vnd, NT1 and Ptx1 genes were not considerably decreased in the absence of Ubx.
source: In contrast, H3K27me3 levels at Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci associated with the vnd, NT1 and Ptx1 genes were not considerably decreased
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci associated with vnd, NT1 and Ptx1 had significantly higher H3K27ac levels in the absence of Ubx.
source: however, these loci had significantly higher H3K27ac levels in the absence of Ubx (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the absence of Ubx, Pho's ability to interact with the five Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci was strongly reduced and concomitantly H3K27me3 as well as H3K27ac levels were changed.
source: These results revealed that in the absence of Ubx Pho's ability to interact with the five Ubx/Pho/H3K27me3 loci was strongly reduced and concomitantly H3K27me3 as well as H3K27ac levels were changed.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the ChIP-qPCR results for Pho binding and histone modifications.

claim: In total, 4154 sites experienced a loss/reduction in Pho binding in the absence of Ubx.
source: In total, 4154 sites experienced a loss/reduction in Pho binding in the absence of Ubx (Figure 7A)
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis of Pho ChIP-seq data.

claim: At 3324 sites Pho binding was gained or increased in the absence of Ubx.
source: while at 3324 sites Pho binding was gained or increased (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: 62% (2567/4154) of the regions which lost Pho binding in the absence of Ubx were co-bound by Ubx in control nuclei.
source: Intriguingly, 62% (2567/4154) of the regions, which lost Pho binding in the absence of Ubx, were co-bound by Ubx in control nuclei (Figure 7B)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of regions losing Pho binding with Ubx binding sites.

claim: The co-dependency of Ubx and Pho binding to shared chromatin sites was revealed by the finding that 62% of regions losing Pho binding were co-bound by Ubx.
source: revealing a co-dependency of Ubx and Pho binding to shared chromatin sites.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the high percentage of Pho-loss regions that are also Ubx-bound.

claim: 422 of the 3501 genes associated with Ubx/Pho regions that lost Pho binding were up-regulated in Ubx depleted mesodermal nuclei.
source: Notably, 422 of the 3501 genes associated with Ubx/Pho regions that lost Pho binding were up-regulated in Ubx depleted mesodermal nuclei (Figure 7D)
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of genes near Pho-loss regions with RNA-seq data.

claim: The 422 genes associated with Ubx/Pho regions that lost Pho binding and were up-regulated encoded preferentially proteins controlling alternative fates.
source: which again encoded preferentially proteins controlling alternative fates (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: No significant change of H3K27ac and H3K27me3 levels was detected at Ubx/Pho co-bound sites that lost Pho binding when Ubx was degraded on the global level.
source: Notably, we did not detect any significant change of H3K27ac and H3K27me3 levels at these sites on the global level, which was also the case for Ubx/Pho co-bound sites that did not experience a change in Pho binding when Ubx was degraded (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of histone marks at different categories of Ubx/Pho sites.

claim: A subset of 328 loci which lost Pho binding and were defined as regions experiencing histone changes towards activation showed a highly significant loss of H3K27me3 marks as well as a gain of H3K27ac marks.
source: However, a subset of 328 loci, which lost Pho binding and were defined before as regions experiencing histone changes towards activation (Figure 4D), showed a highly significant loss of H3K27me3 marks (as well as a gain of H3K27ac marks) (Figure 7F)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of histone marks at specific loci shown in Figure 7F.

claim: A substantial number of Ubx/Pho sites required Ubx for stabilizing Pho binding and H3K27me3 marks.
source: demonstrating that a substantial number of Ubx/Pho sites required Ubx for stabilizing Pho binding and H3K27me3 marks.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis of histone mark changes at Pho-loss sites.

claim: Ubx stabilized Pho binding to chromatin regions at alternative fate genes in the mesodermal lineage, which controlled the proper levels of H3K27me3 and H3K27ac marks, thereby ensuring repression of these genes.
source: In sum, these results demonstrated that Ubx stabilized Pho binding to chromatin regions at alternative fate genes in the mesodermal lineage, which controlled the proper levels of H3K27me3 and H3K27ac marks, thereby ensuring repression of these genes.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement integrating multiple lines of evidence from ChIP-seq and RNA-seq experiments.

claim: Multi-lineage TFs of the Hox class stabilize the different lineage choices by restricting cellular plasticity in a lineage specific manner.
source: Here, we provide evidence that multi-lineage TFs of the Hox class stabilize the different lineage choices by restricting cellular plasticity in a lineage specific manner.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main finding based on the comprehensive experimental evidence presented.

claim: Ubx comprehensively orchestrates the transcriptional programs of the mesodermal as well as of the neuronal lineage, as it bound and regulated a substantially fraction of genes specifically expressed in these tissue lineages.
source: Using this experimental set-up, we found that Ubx comprehensively orchestrates the transcriptional programs of the mesodermal as well as of the neuronal lineage, as it bound and regulated a substantially fraction of genes specifically expressed in these tissue lineages.
evidence: The claim is based on the comprehensive ChIP-seq and RNA-seq analysis showing widespread Ubx binding and regulation.

claim: The majority of Ubx chromatin interactions were located in the vicinity of inactive genes.
source: Strikingly, this analysis revealed that the majority of Ubx chromatin interactions were located in the vicinity of inactive genes
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: About 20% of Ubx interactions at inactive genes were important for repressing the close-by genes.
source: and lineage-specific interference with Ubx in the mesoderm demonstrated that about 20% of these interactions were important for repressing the close-by genes.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of genes up-regulated upon Ubx depletion that are also bound by Ubx.

claim: Genes repressed by Ubx at inactive sites were highly enriched for alternative cell fates.
source: Intriguingly, these genes were highly enriched for alternative cell fates, demonstrating that Ubx had indeed a pivotal role in restricting the developmental potential of cell and tissue types in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO term enrichment analysis of up-regulated genes in Ubx depleted mesoderm.

claim: Ubx had a pivotal role in restricting the developmental potential of cell and tissue types in a context-dependent manner.
source: demonstrating that Ubx had indeed a pivotal role in restricting the developmental potential of cell and tissue types in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the finding that Ubx represses alternative fate genes.

claim: Hox TFs cross-regulate each other's expression, a phenomenon described as posterior suppression.
source: First, Hox TFs cross-regulate each other's expression, a phenomenon described as posterior suppression (Morata and Kerridge, 1982; Struhl, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to classic studies on Hox gene regulation.

claim: Antennapedia (Antp) is ectopically activated when Ubx function is absent.
source: Consistently, the Hox gene Antennapedia (Antp), which is normally expressed anterior to Ubx, is ectopically activated when Ubx function is absent (Figure 8—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing ectopic Antp expression in Ubx depleted embryos.

claim: Antp can partially take over the function of Ubx in the mesodermal lineage when Ubx is absent.
source: allowing Antp now to partially take over the function of Ubx in this lineage.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the observation of ectopic Antp expression and known Hox gene redundancy.

claim: The turn-over rates of the histone variant H3.3 at regulatory regions were correlated with specific histone modifications in mammalian cells.
source: Second, gene regulation is tightly linked to the chromatin status at promoter and enhancer regions. It had been shown in mammalian cells that the turn-over rates of the histone variant H3.3 at regulatory regions were correlated with specific histone modifications, high turn-over when associated with high levels of active histone modifications, like H3K27ac, while much slower turn-over when associated with higher levels of H3K27me3 marks (Kraushaar et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study on histone dynamics.

claim: The 'clearing' of repressive histone modifications takes much longer in comparison to active ones.
source: This implies that the 'clearing' of repressive histone modifications takes much longer in comparison to active ones.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cited study on histone turnover rates.

claim: H3K27me3 marks serve as epigenetic memory to permanently silence genes in the course of development.
source: Third, H3K27me3 marks serve as epigenetic memory to permanently silence genes in the course of development
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the function of H3K27me3 marks.

claim: A resetting of the epigenetic status requires cell division to dilute the H3K27me3 mediated silencing effect.
source: and a recent study demonstrated that a resetting of the epigenetic status requires cell division to dilute the H3K27me3 mediated silencing effect (Coleman and Struhl, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study on epigenetic memory.

claim: After its specification at embryonic stage 12 the mesoderm does not divide anymore.
source: However, after its specification at embryonic stage 12 the mesoderm does not divide anymore
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about Drosophila mesoderm development.

claim: The lack of cell division in the mesoderm after stage 12 might prevent an efficient clearing of H3K27me3 marks at Ubx targeted chromatin sites.
source: which might prevent an efficient clearing of H3K27me3 marks at Ubx targeted chromatin sites.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the requirement for cell division to clear H3K27me3 marks.

claim: De-repression of genes requires not only abolishing repression but also gaining activation, which requires a change of the histone environment and the expression and action of the proper sets of TFs.
source: Fourth, de-repression of genes is not only a consequence of abolishing repression but also of gaining activation, which not only requires a change of the histone environment at control regions but also the expression and action of the proper sets of TFs.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about gene regulation mechanisms.

claim: Only about 5% of the TFs expressed in the neuronal lineage were expressed in the Ubx depleted mesodermal cells.
source: Comparing the transcriptomes of the mesodermal and neuronal lineages revealed that only about 5% of the TFs expressed in an alternative lineage, in this case the neuronal one, were expressed in the Ubx depleted mesodermal cells, including vnd, HGTX, ham and Ptx1
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of transcription factor expression between lineages.

claim: The expression of only about 10% of the mesodermal fate related TFs was reduced in Ubx depleted mesodermal cells.
source: in particular as the expression of only about 10% of the mesodermal fate related TFs was reduced in their expression.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of transcription factor expression changes in Ubx depleted mesoderm.

claim: The expression of alternative lineage TFs in Ubx depleted mesoderm was not sufficient to induce a lineage switch.
source: which was obviously not sufficient to induce a lineage switch
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that mesoderm identity is maintained despite expression of some alternative TFs.

claim: Antp is ectopically expressed in the mesodermal lineage in the absence of Ubx and is assumed to partially take over the lineage-specific function of Ubx.
source: As we find Antp to be ectopically expressed in the mesodermal lineage in the absence of Ubx (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), we assume Antp to partially take over the lineage-specific function of Ubx.
evidence: The claim is based on data showing ectopic Antp expression and inference about its functional role.

claim: The Hox TF Ubx lineage-specifically repressed the transcription of alternative fate genes by organizing the epigenetic landscape.
source: Another highly relevant finding of our study is that the Hox TF Ubx lineage-specifically repressed the transcription of alternative fate genes by organizing the epigenetic landscape
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings from histone modification analysis.

claim: Chromatin changes at Ubx sites were dependent on the interaction of Ubx with the Polycomb recruiter Pho.
source: and that chromatin changes at Ubx sites were dependent on the interaction of Ubx with the Polycomb recruiter Pho (Henry et al., 2012; Schoenfelder et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data on Ubx-Pho interaction and histone changes, and citations to previous studies on Pho function.

claim: Ubx was crucial for stabilizing binding of the PcG protein Pho to specific chromatin regions.
source: Strikingly, our study revealed that Ubx was crucial for stabilizing binding of the PcG protein Pho to specific chromatin regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing loss of Pho binding when Ubx is depleted.

claim: DNA binding TFs other than Pho interact with PREs, for example Grainyhead.
source: Although it is known that DNA binding TFs other than Pho interact with PREs, for example Grainyhead (Kassis and Brown, 2013; Müller and Kassis, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on PRE-binding factors.

claim: Grainyhead has been shown recently to lineage-specifically displace nucleosomes at enhancers.
source: a TF that has been shown recently to lineage-specifically displace nucleosomes at enhancers (Jacobs et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study on Grainyhead function.

claim: Previous studies on TF interactions with PREs were mostly performed in vitro and the role of these TFs in Pho chromatin targeting was not addressed.
source: these studies were mostly performed in vitro and the role of these TFs in Pho chromatin targeting was not addressed (Nishioka et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation and characterizes the limitations of previous studies.

claim: The combinatorial interaction of Ubx and Pho on the chromatin was analysed in vivo, in the mesodermal lineage of Drosophila embryos.
source: In contrast, we analysed the combinatorial interaction of Ubx and Pho on the chromatin in vivo, in the mesodermal lineage of Drosophila embryos.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental approach used in this study.

claim: Pho was no longer able to interact with Ubx bound sites when Ubx protein was depleted in a lineage-specific manner, while Pho-only chromatin interactions were unaffected.
source: Importantly, we showed that Pho was no longer able to interact with Ubx bound sites when Ubx protein was depleted in a lineage-specific manner, while Pho-only chromatin interactions were unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data comparing Pho binding in control and Ubx depleted conditions.

claim: As a result of Pho loss from Ubx sites, H3K27me3 levels were reduced and H3K27ac levels increased, resulting in the de-repression of genes primarily associated with Ubx-Pho chromatin regions.
source: As a result, H3K27me3 levels were reduced and H3K27ac levels increased, resulting in the de-repression of genes primarily associated with Ubx-Pho chromatin regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by histone ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: Not only Pho but very likely the whole PcG protein complex was not properly targeted to Ubx chromatin sites when Ubx was depleted.
source: This result indicated that not only Pho but very likely the whole PcG protein complex was not properly targeted to Ubx chromatin sites
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the loss of Pho binding and H3K27me3 marks, which is deposited by the PcG complex.

claim: The inference that the whole PcG complex is not properly targeted is in line with the finding that H3K27me3 levels were generally decreased at enhancers of genes de-repressed upon Ubx depletion.
source: which is in line with our finding that H3K27me3 levels were generally decreased at enhancers of genes de-repressed upon Ubx depletion (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim connects the inference about PcG complex targeting with the observed histone modification changes.

claim: H3K27ac levels increased at Ubx chromatin interactions located in the vicinity of de-repressed genes.
source: However, we also found H3K27ac levels increased at Ubx chromatin interactions located in the vicinity of de-repressed genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by histone ChIP-seq data.

claim: PREs frequently co-localize with response elements for Trithorax group (TrxG) proteins.
source: Interestingly, PREs frequently co-localize with response elements for Trithorax group (TrxG) proteins (Kingston and Tamkun, 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a review on chromatin regulation.

claim: The binding motif for the GAGA TF Trithorax-like (Trl) was identified enriched among the Ubx bound and H3K27me3 marked chromatin sites.
source: In this line, we identified not only the binding motif for Pho but also for the GAGA TF Trithorax-like (Trl) enriched among the Ubx bound and H3K27me3 marked chromatin sites
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Trl interacted with Ubx in cellulo.
source: and we found Trl to interact with Ubx in cellulo (Figure 8—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Trl was initially discovered to activate transcription, in particular of the Ubx gene.
source: Trl was initially discovered to activate transcription, in particular of the Ubx gene (Biggin and Tjian, 1988)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the original study on Trl function.

claim: Trl is also required for transcriptional repression, as it binds PREs.
source: but is also required for transcriptional repression, as it binds PREs (Horard et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on Trl binding to PREs.

claim: Trl physically associates with the Polycomb Repressive Complex 1.
source: and physically associates with the Polycomb Repressive Complex 1 (Poux et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a study on Trl-PRC1 interaction.

claim: Trl had been suggested recently to function as a pioneer factor in early Drosophila development by making genomic regions accessible through the deposition of active histone marks.
source: Interestingly, Trl had been suggested recently to function as a pioneer factor in early Drosophila development by making genomic regions accessible through the deposition of active histone marks.
evidence: The claim is based on recent literature on Trl function, though no specific citation is provided in this sentence.

claim: The methyltransferase Trithorax (Trx) mediates together with the p300/CREB-binding protein (CBP) the deposition of H3K27ac marks.
source: Furthermore, it had been shown that another TrxG protein, the methyltransferase Trithorax (Trx), mediates together with the p300/CREB-binding protein (CBP) the deposition of H3K27ac marks (Tie et al., 2016; Tie et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on Trx and CBP function.

claim: H3K27ac marks were enriched at promoters and enhancers upon Ubx depletion.
source: a histone mark that was enriched at promoters and enhancers upon Ubx depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by histone ChIP-seq data.

claim: The TrxG complex and CBP could be recruited in the absence of Ubx to activate gene expression.
source: Thus, the TrxG complex and CBP could be recruited in the absence of Ubx to activate gene expression (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the increase in H3K27ac marks and known functions of TrxG and CBP.

claim: GAGA factors are required for the formation of repressive chromatin loops in Polycomb domains to stabilize gene silencing during early Drosophila development.
source: Interestingly, a recent study showed that GAGA factors are required for the formation of repressive chromatin loops in Polycomb domains to stabilize gene silencing during early Drosophila development (Ogiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study on GAGA factor function.

claim: The increase of H3K27me3 marks in the absence of Ubx could be due to Trl interacting with these sites when Ubx levels drop, thereby promoting or increasing the formation of repressive chromatin loops.
source: These results could explain one puzzling result of our study, the increase of H3K27me3 marks in the absence of Ubx, which could be due to Trl interacting with these sites when Ubx levels drop (Figure 8), thereby promoting or increasing the formation of repressive chromatin loops.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis to explain the observed increase in H3K27me3 at some sites.

claim: Tissue-specific TFs like Snail (Sna) in the mesoderm and Ventral nervous system defective (Vnd) in the neuronal lineage provide specificity to Hox TF function.
source: One explanation is that tissue/lineage restricted factors and their interaction with Hox TFs provide specificity. Interestingly, we find the binding motif for the mesoderm-specific TF Snail (Sna) enriched among the sites, which are bound by Ubx and marked by H3K27me3 in the mesodermal lineage, while in the neuronal lineage the Ventral nervous system defective (Vnd) motif is frequently found in Ubx/H3K27me3 sites.
evidence: The claim is based on motif enrichment analysis showing lineage-specific TF motifs at Ubx binding sites.

claim: Motifs for tissue-specific TFs are also detected at active Ubx sites, as Ubx/H3K27ac regions in the mesoderm have the Slouch (Slou) motif enriched, while in the nervous system it is the motif for Intermediate neuroblasts defective (Ind).
source: Motifs for tissue-specific TFs are also detected at active sites, as Ubx/H3K27ac regions in the mesoderm have the Slouch (Slou) motif enriched, while in the nervous system it is the motif for Intermediate neuroblasts defective (Ind).
evidence: The claim is based on motif enrichment analysis at active Ubx binding sites.

claim: Tissue-restricted factors are assumed to be critical in determining the lineage-specific output of Hox TFs.
source: Thus, we assume these factors to be critical in determining the lineage-specific output (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the enrichment of tissue-specific TF motifs at Ubx binding sites.

claim: Hox TFs are not only active during development but their input is continuously required throughout the lifetime of an organism to assess the positional values of cells and to maintain their proper identities and functions.
source: One peculiar feature of Hox TFs is that they are not only active during the development but their input is continuously required throughout the lifetime of an organism to assess the positional values of cells and to maintain their proper identities and functions (Argiropoulos and Humphries, 2007; Cerdá-Esteban and Spagnoli, 2014; Friedrich et al., 2016; Leucht et al., 2008; Morgan, 2006; Philippidou and Dasen, 2013; Philippidou et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies on Hox gene function in development and maintenance.

claim: Hox TFs robustly repress alternative lineage programs via interaction with epigenetic factors like Pho and reliably restrict the developmental potential encoded in cells.
source: Our findings now shed new light on the mechanism ensuring this stability in cellular identity, as they suggest that Hox TFs robustly repress alternative lineage programs (via the interaction with epigenetic factors like Pho) and reliably restrict the developmental potential encoded cells.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the main mechanistic finding of the study.

claim: In the normal context, Hox-mediated restriction of developmental potential is absolutely critical for an organism to function properly.
source: In the normal context, this is absolutely critical for an organism to function properly
evidence: The claim is based on general biological knowledge about the importance of cell identity maintenance.

claim: Hox-mediated restriction of developmental potential can be a major hurdle when cells need or should adopt a new identity, which requires them to regain plasticity.
source: however, in some instances it can be a major hurdle, in particular when cells need or should adopt a new identity, which requires them often to regain plasticity.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis about the implications of Hox-mediated restriction for cellular reprogramming.

claim: Cellular reprogramming, which is extensively studied due to its high potential as therapeutic strategy, is still inefficient.
source: Another situation of cell type conversion is cellular reprogramming, which is extensively studied due to its high potential as therapeutic strategy (Lin et al., 2018). But although reprogramming strategies have been improved over time, the direct conversion of one somatic cell type into another one, the so-called transdifferentiation, is still inefficient (Ebert et al., 2015; Manandhar et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent reviews on cellular reprogramming.

claim: The induction of the Hox code typical for a differentiated cell type in pluripotent stem cells (PSCs), either in combination with other factors or even alone, can convert PSCs into the cell type expressing the Hox code in vivo.
source: Interestingly, it has been reported recently that the induction of the Hox code typical for a differentiated cell type in pluripotent stem cells (PSCs), either in combination (Sugimura et al., 2017) with other factors or even alone (Steens et al., 2017), can convert PSCs into the cell type expressing the Hox code in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to recent studies on Hox-mediated cell type conversion.

claim: Hox genes can effectively induce cell type specific transcriptional programs in multi-potent cells thereby unambiguously inducing their differentiation.
source: This clearly shows that Hox genes can effectively induce cell type specific transcriptional programs in multi-potent cells thereby unambiguously inducing their differentiation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cited studies showing Hox-mediated cell type conversion.

claim: This finding is in line with the study's findings showing that Hox TFs activate lineage-specific transcriptional profiles with high precision.
source: This is in line with our findings showing that Hox TFs activate lineage-specific transcriptional profiles with high precision.
